frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.
Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).
4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser for home use if they perceive it as a health‑monitoring tool that provides measurable, reliable body‑fat data, because they value evidence‑based health decisions.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who want to track body fat for weight management, fitness, or medical monitoring.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers learn that the device measures body fat with a validated method (e.g., Tanita’s 0.8 kg bias relative to a four‑compartment model), they will be motivated to purchase it for personal health tracking.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the device at a premium price justified by its accuracy and by licensing the technology to other consumer brands for health‑tracking features.
assumptions: Consumers trust medical‑grade accuracy when they see a validated measurement method.
Health‑conscious consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides measurable body‑fat data.
The device can be marketed as a health‑monitoring tool rather than just a scale.
predictions: If a survey of health‑conscious consumers shows >30% would purchase a stand‑on BIA analyser for home use, the theory is supported.
If a controlled test shows purchase intent increases when accuracy is highlighted, the theory is supported.
If a competitor launches a similar device without accuracy claims, consumer demand may be limited.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers learn the device provides rapid, reliable body‑fat measurement and can be used in the privacy of their home, they will be motivated to purchase it for daily health tracking.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the device at a premium price justified by its speed and convenience, and by licensing the technology to other consumer brands for health‑tracking features.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and speed over accuracy when choosing health monitoring tools.
The device can be marketed as a time‑saving, at‑home solution rather than a medical tool.
There is a market segment willing to pay for a device that fits their lifestyle.
predictions: If a survey of health‑conscious consumers shows >30% would purchase a stand‑on BIA analyser for home use, the theory is supported.
If a controlled test shows purchase intent increases when convenience is highlighted, the theory is supported.
If a competitor launches a similar device without convenience claims, consumer demand may be limited.

X1.name: Home Health Monitoring Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 200 health‑conscious adults (18-55) recruited via health forums and social media, balanced for gender and BMI range.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale (1‑very unlikely, 10‑very likely). 2) WTP in euros for a stand‑on BIA analyser (median value). 3) Self‑reported importance of accuracy vs. convenience vs. other factors.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent and WTP will be higher when accuracy is emphasized (e.g., "validated medical measurement").
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent and WTP will be higher when convenience is emphasized (e.g., "rapid, at‑home health check").

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the accuracy‑focused scenario is at least 7.5 (out of 10) and the WTP is at least €150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing accuracy. If purchase intent for the convenience‑focused scenario is at least 7.5 and WTP is at least €150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If neither meets both thresholds, do not invest.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer demand, accuracy, or convenience. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a limited test (e.g., the proposed 10‑week survey) to validate consumer demand and willingness to pay before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious adults (18‑55) who value evidence‑based health decisions and are willing to pay a premium for accurate body‑fat measurement.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on body‑fat analyser marketed as a medical‑grade health‑monitoring tool, emphasizing validated accuracy and reliability, with a premium price justified by its precision.
final.next_action: Run the Home Health Monitoring Preference Test (200 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under accuracy vs. convenience framing.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a stand‑on BIA analyser is uncertain; the test will clarify whether health‑conscious buyers are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent ≥7.5 and WTP ≥€150 for the accuracy‑focused scenario, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition emphasizing accuracy.
If the test shows purchase intent ≥7.5 and WTP ≥€150 for the convenience‑focused scenario, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition emphasizing convenience.
If neither meets both thresholds, we would not invest.

position.recommendation: Proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor enthusiasts, campers, and boat owners, leveraging ACR’s existing 406 MHz technology and brand reputation for reliability. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Individual marine recreational users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because they need reliable emergency communication and are willing to pay a premium for a device that can be used by friends and family.
T1.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher-margin consumer sales and brand awareness.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Recreational mariners currently lack affordable, reliable emergency communication tools; a dedicated consumer product would address this gap and signal safety commitment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR would sell the beacon directly to consumers at premium prices, capturing value through higher unit margins and brand positioning as a safety essential.
assumptions: Recreational mariners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a dedicated emergency beacon.
They are aware of the 406 MHz beacon technology and its capabilities.
They trust ACR's reputation for maritime safety products.
predictions: Surveyed recreational mariners will express intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $100.
Sales of a consumer beacon will be higher in regions with high recreational boating activity.
ACR's market share in the consumer segment will be measurable within 12 months of launch.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., 12‑week online survey with willingness-to-pay questions) to validate demand among marine recreational users before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a reliable, life-saving tool for remote emergencies, and are willing to pay a premium for a dedicated consumer product.
T1.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margins and brand equity by selling a differentiated consumer product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Users will switch from relying on traditional methods (phone, radio) to a beacon when they understand it can be activated in remote areas where cellular coverage is absent, and it is certified by NOAA and RTCM.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales at premium prices, leveraging its existing B2B reputation to signal safety and reliability.
assumptions: Consumers trust NOAA certification and RTCM standards as indicators of safety.
Price sensitivity is low for a single emergency device used once.
Marketing can communicate the beacon’s unique ability to reach rescue satellites in remote areas.
predictions: Surveyed marine recreational users will indicate intent to purchase a beacon at a price 20% above standard PLBs.
Pilot sales in a test market will show at least 5% conversion rate among targeted users.
Competitor products will not capture a significant share of the consumer market due to ACR’s established safety reputation.
T1.first_claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a reliable, life-saving tool for remote emergencies, and are willing to pay a premium for a dedicated consumer product.

T2.claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a convenient, one‑time purchase for outdoor activities, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that eliminates the need to carry multiple emergency tools.
T2.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margins and brand awareness by selling a consumer‑focused, single‑use product.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Users will adopt a beacon when it offers a single, reliable way to signal distress in remote areas, reducing the need to carry multiple devices (e.g., phone, radio, flashlight). The convenience of a single device drives purchase.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales at premium prices, leveraging its existing B2B reputation to position the beacon as a safety essential for outdoor enthusiasts.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over cost for a single emergency device.
Marketing can emphasize the beacon’s single activation and its suitability for outdoor activities.
The device is perceived as a one‑time purchase rather than a recurring subscription service.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a beacon at a price 15% above standard PLBs.
Pilot sales in a test market will show at least 8% conversion rate among targeted users.
Competitor products will not capture a significant share of the consumer market due to ACR’s established outdoor safety reputation.
T2.first_claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a convenient, one‑time purchase for outdoor activities, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that eliminates the need to carry multiple emergency tools.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Emergency vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users (recruited via outdoor forums) and 150 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor lifestyle platforms). Stratified to reflect age and gender distribution.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) or likelihood to choose a premium price (0-100% scale). 2) Maximum price willing to pay (EUR) for a differentiated consumer proposition. 3) Primary motivation (emergency vs convenience) selected from a 5-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Surveyed marine users will report purchase intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% above standard PLB price; outdoor enthusiasts will report intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 15% above standard PLB price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will report purchase intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 15% above standard PLB price; marine users will report intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% above standard PLB price.

X1.decision_rule: If marine users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium AND outdoor users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 15% premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (T1 favored). If outdoor users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 15% premium AND marine users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (T2 favored). If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or purchase behavior for a differentiated consumer proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., 12‑week online survey with willingness‑to‑pay questions) to validate demand among marine recreational users before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Marine recreational users (outdoor boaters, sailors, and recreational fishermen) who need reliable emergency signaling in remote areas.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product that leverages ACR’s 406 MHz satellite distress‑beacon technology, marketed as a NOAA‑certified, RTCM‑compliant emergency signal device specifically designed for marine use, offering reliable distress alert
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (300 respondents, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay among marine users. If intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% premium, proceed to develop a consumer
final.uncertainty: The size of the marine recreational market and its willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated product are unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the pilot test shows marine users’ intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% premium, we would recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition.
If the pilot test shows marine users’ intent below 40% or willingness to pay below 10% premium, we would recommend no expansion.

arguments.claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a reliable, life-saving tool for remote emergencies, and are willing to pay a premium for a dedicated consumer product.
arguments.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margins and brand equity by selling a differentiated consumer product.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Users will switch from relying on traditional methods (phone, radio) to a beacon when they understand it can be activated in remote areas where cellular coverage is absent, and it is certified by NOAA and RTCM.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales at premium prices, leveraging its existing B2B reputation to signal safety and reliability.
assumptions: Consumers trust NOAA certification and RTCM standards as indicators of safety.
Price sensitivity is low for a single emergency device used once.
Marketing can communicate the beacon’s unique ability to reach rescue satellites in remote areas.
predictions: Surveyed marine recreational users will indicate intent to purchase a beacon at a price 20% above standard PLBs.
Pilot sales in a test market will show at least 5% conversion rate among targeted users.
Competitor products will not capture a significant share of the consumer market due to ACR’s established safety reputation.

arguments.claim: Individual users will adopt 406 MHz satellite distress beacons if they perceive them as a convenient, one‑time purchase for outdoor activities, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that eliminates the need to carry multiple emergency tools.
arguments.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margins and brand awareness by selling a consumer‑focused, single‑use product.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Users will adopt a beacon when it offers a single, reliable way to signal distress in remote areas, reducing the need to carry multiple devices (e.g., phone, radio, flashlight). The convenience of a single device drives purchase.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales at premium prices, leveraging its existing B2B reputation to position the beacon as a safety essential for outdoor enthusiasts.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over cost for a single emergency device.
Marketing can emphasize the beacon’s single activation and its suitability for outdoor activities.
The device is perceived as a one‑time purchase rather than a recurring subscription service.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a beacon at a price 15% above standard PLBs.
Pilot sales in a test market will show at least 8% conversion rate among targeted users.
Competitor products will not capture a significant share of the consumer market due to ACR’s established outdoor safety reputation.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Emergency vs Convenience Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users (recruited via outdoor forums) and 150 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor lifestyle platforms). Stratified to reflect age and gender distribution.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) or likelihood to choose a premium price (0-100% scale). 2) Maximum price willing to pay (EUR) for a differentiated consumer proposition. 3) Primary motivation (emergency vs convenience) selected from a 5-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Surveyed marine users will report purchase intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% above standard PLB price; outdoor enthusiasts will report intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 15% above standard PLB price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will report purchase intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 15% above standard PLB price; marine users will report intent ≥ 60% and willingness to pay at least 20% above standard PLB price.

arguments.decision_rule: If marine users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium AND outdoor users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 15% premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (T1 favored). If outdoor users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 15% premium AND marine users’ intent ≥ 60% AND willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (T2 favored). If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., 12‑week online survey with willingness-to-pay questions) to validate demand among marine recreational users before committing resources.

If the pilot test shows marine users’ intent below 40% or willingness to pay below 10% premium, we would recommend no expansion.

tool_result.question: It is late 2002. Should ACR Electronics develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology? What evidence would justify that investment?
tool_result.brief: ACR Electronics is a Fort Lauderdale maker of emergency radio beacons for ships and aircraft and of survival lights for military and commercial marine users. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

X1.method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A sees a status‑focused lawn tractor description emphasizing prestige, convenience, and brand prestige; Condition B sees a reliability‑focused description emphasizing ease of use, durability, and trust from farm equipment. Both conditions present the same product details (e.g., 110 model, basic attachments). Participants indicate whether they would purchase at a price point of $2,500 and provide a reason. Data are analyzed to compare purchase intent and reason across conditions.
X1.sample: 300 homeowners aged 25–65 with household income over $50,000, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assign 150 to Condition A and 150 to Condition B.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and status/reason in Condition A (status‑focused).

If neither difference meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B2C model.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Reliability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase decisions and choice-based conjoint. Participants view two product concepts (A and B) with identical technical specifications but differing messaging: Concept A emphasizes status and convenience (e.g., "Modern lawn tractor for the homeowner, perfect for landscaping and showing off your garden.") Concept B emphasizes reliability and ease of use (e.g., "Durable, easy-to-use tractor for light gardening and small tasks.") Participants indicate which concept they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The test is limited to 500 participants, 12 weeks, and costs €20,000.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25-55 with a household income above the median, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by geographic region to reflect 1962 U.S. market distribution.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: percentage choosing Concept A over B. 2) Maximum price willingness to pay: average amount participants indicate they would pay for Concept A. 3) Primary purchase reason: open-ended survey question identifying whether participants cite status/convenience (T1) or reliability/ease of use (T2).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Concept A will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for A will be at least 20% higher than for B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Concept B will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for B will be at least 20% higher than for A.

X1.decision_rule: If Concept A’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than Concept B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing status and convenience. If Concept B’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than A, develop a proposition emphasizing reliability and ease of use. If neither threshold is met, abandon expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain the existing B2B2C model and continue leveraging independent dealers to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale test (e.g., a limited launch of a basic consumer line) to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Homeowners aged 25-55 with disposable income, located in the United States, who need a reliable, easy-to-use tool for small-scale landscaping and gardening.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes status and convenience, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering to offer a premium, brand‑rich lawn tractor sold through independent dealers with financing and service.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and price willingness for a status‑focused concept versus a reliability‑focused concept.
final.uncertainty: The actual demand for a differentiated consumer proposition in 1962 is unknown; the test will resolve this. Also uncertain is whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for status and convenience compared to reliability.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the status concept ≥ 55% and price willingness at least 20% higher than for the reliability concept, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.

If the test shows purchase intent for the reliability concept ≥ 55% and price willingness at least 20% higher than for the status concept, we would develop a proposition emphasizing reliability and ease of use.
If neither threshold is met, we would abandon expansion and continue the B2B2C model.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Status vs. Reliability Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase decisions and choice-based conjoint. Participants view two product concepts (A and B) with identical technical specifications but differing messaging: Concept A emphasizes status and convenience (e.g., "Modern lawn tractor for the homeowner, perfect for landscaping and showing off your garden.") Concept B emphasizes reliability and ease of use (e.g., "Durable, easy-to-use tractor for light gardening and small tasks.") Participants indicate which concept they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The test is limited to 500 participants, 12 weeks, and costs €20,000.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25-55 with a household income above the median, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by geographic region to reflect 1962 U.S. market distribution.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: percentage choosing Concept A over B. 2) Maximum price willingness to pay: average amount participants indicate they would pay for Concept A. 3) Primary purchase reason: open-ended survey question identifying whether participants cite status/convenience (T1) or reliability/ease of use (T2).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Concept A will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for A will be at least 20% higher than for B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Concept B will be chosen by at least 55% of participants, and the average price willingness for B will be at least 20% higher than for A.

arguments.decision_rule: If Concept A’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than Concept B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing status and convenience. If Concept B’s purchase intent ≥ 55% and its average price willingness ≥ 20% higher than A, develop a proposition emphasizing reliability and ease of use. If neither threshold is met, abandon expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes status and convenience, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering to offer a premium, brand‑rich lawn tractor sold through independent dealers with financing and service.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two distinct ad copy versions. Participants view a description of a lawn tractor, either emphasizing low cost and convenience (T1) or emphasizing status and brand prestige (T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this tractor if offered at a price comparable to existing garden tools?"
X1.sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for region (Midwest, Northeast, California) and household income (low, moderate, high).
X1.measure: Purchase intent binary (yes/no) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) on a 0–10 scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP when the ad emphasizes low cost and convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP when the ad emphasizes status and brand prestige.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the low‑cost/convenience version exceeds the status version by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who value convenience. If the difference is <15 points or not significant, consider no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer motivations for lawn tractors or the feasibility of a direct-to-consumer proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a low-cost, easy-to-use tool for light landscaping.
final.value_proposition: A lawn tractor sold directly to consumers at a price comparable to existing garden tools, offering convenience, reliability, and Deere’s brand reputation, capturing value through retail margins and brand premium.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (400 households, 8 weeks, €8,000) to compare low‑cost/convenience messaging versus status/brand messaging. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer line.

arguments.value_proposition: A lawn tractor sold directly to consumers at a price comparable to existing garden tools, offering convenience, reliability, and Deere’s brand reputation, capturing value through retail margins and brand premium.

tool_result.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?
tool_result.brief: Deere & Company is an Illinois maker of farm tractors, combines and industrial equipment sold through a network of independent dealers. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.
